strengths: Novel and elegant approach: Adapting polynomial neural networks via a symmetric CP decomposition and progressive training to create nested, dynamic activation probes is a creative solution that naturally bridges linear probes and expressive non-linear models.

Dual dynamic inference modes: The paper convincingly demonstrates two practical operating regimes—a 'safety dial' for user-specified compute budgets and a confidence-based early-exit cascade that achieves full-model performance with near-linear-probe average inference cost.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is tested across multiple LLM families and scales (Llama-3.2-3B, gpt-oss-20b, Gemma-3-27B-it, Qwen3-30B) and two standard safety benchmarks (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails), with thorough hyperparameter tuning and parameter-matched baselines (linear probes, bilinear probes, MLPs, and early-exit MLPs).
Mechanistic interpretability: Unlike black-box MLPs, the low-rank symmetric formulation allows exact, closed-form attribution of safety decisions back to specific pairwise neuron-neuron interactions.

Extensive ablations and practical validation: The appendix provides exhaustive ablations (e.g., rank sweeps, maximum degree analysis, progressive vs. joint training, symmetric vs. unconstrained CP) and real hardware latency/throughput measurements across varying batch sizes.
weaknesses: Contextualization of probe compute vs. backbone compute: Because extracting residual stream activations requires running the LLM forward pass up to layer L, the computational cost of any probe is already minuscule compared to the LLM backbone (<0.01% of parameters). The paper would benefit from explicitly discussing the practical systems-level throughput impact when embedded in an LLM inference pipeline.

Modest overall aggregate gains: While subcategory improvements are noteworthy (up to ~10% accuracy on specific harm types), overall benchmark F1 gains over well-tuned linear probes are often within 1–2 percentage points.

Human interpretability of raw neuron pairs: While mathematically exact and faithful, pairwise neuron attributions in dense activation space remain difficult for humans to interpret without projection onto sparse autoencoder (SAE) dictionaries or semantic concepts, a limitation that could be discussed more prominently.

strengths: Clear motivation and conceptually clean framework: extending linear probes to truncated polynomial classifiers (TPCs) provides an elegant way to trade off inference compute and classification capacity dynamically.

Sound training methodology: the progressive greedy training strategy effectively solves the issue of truncated sub-model performance degradation that standard joint training suffers from, ensuring every truncation order serves as a viable classifier.

Comprehensive experimental validation: evaluation covers two large-scale safety benchmarks (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails) across four contemporary LLMs and multiple layers, thoroughly benchmarking against parameter-matched linear, bilinear, MLP, and early-exit MLP baselines.

Extensive ablations: the authors provide rigorous ablations on rank R, maximum polynomial order N, symmetric vs. unconstrained CP factorization, calibration (ECE), and empirical runtime latency/throughput.
Interpretability: the symmetric CP formulation naturally groups permutationally identical monomials, allowing exact, closed-form attribution of logit shifts to specific pairwise neuron interactions.
weaknesses: Practical bottleneck perspective: while dynamic probe compute is theoretically neat, probe inference accounts for an infinitesimal fraction of total compute compared to the LLM's forward pass (generating the representations). The operational latency/cost savings of cascading a probe are thus minor in end-to-end serving pipelines.

Marginal empirical gains over EE-MLP: although TPC matches or slightly outperforms early-exit MLPs across various settings, the performance delta in terms of overall F1 is often quite narrow (under 1% in many test scenarios).

Human legibility of attributions: while mathematically faithful, raw neuron-level pairwise attributions remain dense and challenging for humans to interpret without further decomposition into monosemantic features (e.g., Sparse Autoencoder latents), as LLM residual stream neurons are largely polysemantic.

Dynamic early-exit batching overhead: dynamic early-exit cascades introduce sample-dependent branching, which can lead to GPU warp divergence or complex batch management in high-throughput production environments.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing an important practical challenge in LLM safety: providing adaptive, compute-flexible safety monitors rather than fixed-cost static probes or expensive LLM-as-judge models.
Technically clean formulation: using symmetric CP decomposition to reduce parameter count to $O(RD)$ and make polynomial evaluation computationally tractable via simple powers of projections.

Comprehensive and thorough empirical evaluation across multiple LLMs (Gemma, Llama, Qwen, GPT-OSS), two safety benchmarks (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails), multiple layers, and extensive rank/order ablations.
Ablations on progressive training validate that greedy term-by-term optimization is necessary to make truncated intermediate sub-models effective classifiers.
Rigorous parameter-matching and dedicated hyperparameter tuning for baseline comparisons, including early-exit MLPs (EE-MLPs) and calibration analysis.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core components—symmetric CP polynomial parameterization (Dubey et al., 2022), greedy progressive training (Belilovsky et al., 2019), and confidence-thresholded early exiting (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016)—are established techniques assembled for probe-based classification.

Modest empirical advantage over standard non-linear early-exit baselines: across most benchmark curves (Figure 2, Figure 6, and Figures 17–19), TPCs achieve nearly identical aggregate F1 scores to parameter-matched EE-MLPs, with noticeable gains isolated only to specific subcategories.

Real-time deployment latency penalty: as shown in the latency benchmark (Figure 12), EE-MLP achieves lower latency than TPC at batch size = 1, which represents the standard operational setting for online, user-facing prompt safety moderation.

Scope is restricted to mean-pooled prompt representations: the method only evaluates sequence-level prompt classification offline and does not monitor auto-regressive generation token-by-token, which is critical for preventing jailbreaks and toxic completions during decoding.

Interpretability benefits remain mostly theoretical: while pairwise interactions can be computed in closed form (Equation 6), raw LLM neurons are highly polysemantic and uninterpretable in isolation, making dense neuron-pair attribution difficult for human moderators to act upon without sparse dictionary features (e.g., SAEs).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework: extending linear activation probes into truncated polynomial classifiers (TPCs) to enable dynamic, compute-flexible safety monitoring.

Methodologically sound approach: using symmetric CP tensor decomposition to manage parameter growth and proposing a progressive training scheme so that lower-order sub-models remain performant and nested.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: evaluated across four diverse modern LLMs (up to 30B parameters), two primary safety datasets, and three out-of-distribution evaluation datasets.

Extensive ablations and baseline fairness: parameter-matching against both independent MLPs and early-exit MLPs (EE-MLP), alongside thorough sweeps over rank, maximum degree, threshold tau, latency/throughput, and layers.
Inherent transparency: polynomial formulation naturally yields exact second-order interaction attribution between activation dimensions/neurons without needing external perturbation methods.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical gains over MLP baselines: while TPCs match or slightly exceed EE-MLPs and standard MLPs on WildGuardMix, EE-MLP matches or slightly outperforms TPC on BeaverTails test F1, indicating that performance differences between polynomial and neural probe architectures are relatively narrow.

Practical significance of probe compute scaling: probing costs (on the order of 1M parameters / few FLOPs) are already minuscule compared to running the base LLM forward pass (e.g., 20B–30B parameters). While the adaptive cascade saves probe compute, the bottleneck in real-world deployment is typically the base model execution, somewhat lessening the practical impact of early-exiting within the probe itself.

Interpretability legibility: as acknowledged in the limitations, while the pairwise interaction weights are mathematically exact and faithful, raw residual stream neuron dimensions are polysemantic and dense, making human auditing of the resulting attributions challenging without sparse feature bases (e.g., SAEs).

strengths: Well-motivated framing: Safety monitoring represents a compelling use-case for dynamic inference-time compute, addressing the gap between static, inflexible linear probes and computationally expensive LLM-as-judge guardrails.

Methodological clarity: The paper presents an elegant formulation of Truncated Polynomial Classifiers (TPCs), combining symmetric CP tensor decomposition with greedy progressive training to create nested, dynamically scalable sub-classifiers.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Experiments span four recent LLM families (Gemma-3-27B, Qwen3-30B, Llama-3.2-3B, GPT-OSS-20B) across two safety benchmarks (WildGuardMix and BeaverTails), complemented by extensive ablations on rank, maximum degree, layer depth, latency/throughput, and calibration.

Inherent mechanistic interpretability: Unlike black-box MLPs, low-to-moderate degree TPCs enable direct, closed-form calculation of pairwise neuron interaction contributions, providing transparent attribution without post-hoc approximation.
weaknesses: Modest overall performance improvements over non-linear baselines: While TPCs outperform linear probes, their overall F1 gains over parameter-matched early-exit MLPs (EE-MLPs) and standard MLPs are narrow (often within 0.2–0.7% F1 on benchmark test sets in Table 1). The larger improvements highlighted (e.g., up to 10%) occur only on specific subcategories.

Latency characteristics in low-batch settings: As shown in Figure 13, for batch size 1 (a standard regime for interactive, user-facing LLM request monitoring), EE-MLP exhibits lower latency across exit orders compared to TPC, which somewhat offsets the computational efficiency argument for online deployment.

Human interpretability of raw neuron attributions: While mathematically exact, attributing decisions to individual dense residual-stream neurons is difficult to interpret semantically without grounding in interpretable representations (e.g., Sparse Autoencoder features), as acknowledged in the limitations.

Incremental technical novelty: Symmetric CP factorizations for polynomials and progressive/greedy layer-wise training have been explored previously; the primary novelty lies in adapting and combining these techniques for dynamic LLM activation monitoring.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework: The paper addresses an important practical problem in LLM safety guardrails—the rigidity and cost trade-off between cheap linear probes and expensive LLM-as-judge monitors—by introducing dynamic, compute-scalable activation monitoring.

Sound technical methodology: The formulation of Truncated Polynomial Classifiers (TPCs) using symmetric low-rank CP tensor decomposition together with greedy progressive training effectively prevents degradation of lower-degree truncations while keeping parameter counts manageable.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span four diverse LLM families (up to 30B parameters), two large safety datasets (WildGuardMix and BeaverTails), thorough baseline comparisons (parameter-matched MLPs, early-exit MLPs, bilinear probes), across multiple layers and ranks.
Dual deployment modes: The demonstrated support for both budget-constrained fixed truncation and input-adaptive cascading (Algorithm 1) provides practical utility for real-world serving systems.

Inherent feature attribution: Unlike black-box MLPs, TPCs retain closed-form attribution to specific pairwise neuron interactions (Eq. 6), adding mechanistic transparency to the guardrail predictions.
weaknesses: Incremental performance margin over early-exit MLPs: In several benchmarks (e.g., Table 1 on BeaverTails and various plots in Fig. 6/8), TPCs achieve performance that is very comparable to, or occasionally slightly below, parameter-matched early-exit MLPs (EE-MLPs). The practical advantage stems primarily from architectural simplicity and attribution rather than pure predictive superiority.

Practical latency at batch size 1: The latency and throughput benchmarks in Appendix G.2 (Fig. 13) reveal that at batch size 1—which is common for real-time interactive LLM serving—EE-MLPs exhibit lower latency than TPCs. TPCs only become faster at large batch sizes (e.g., 1024+), which somewhat tempers the latency argument for real-time edge or low-concurrency deployments.

Human interpretability of raw neuron interactions: While Eq. (6) provides mechanistically faithful attribution to pairs of residual stream dimensions, residual stream neurons in modern LLMs are polysemantic and dense, making the raw attributions difficult to interpret semantically without projecting onto Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features.

Reliance on simple mean-pooling: The method averages token representations across the full prompt ($z = \frac{1}{T}\sum h_t$), which may dilute localized harmful signals or triggers compared to position-specific probing (e.g., last-token residual stream).
